lesson_title: Two People Counting the Same Money: Bank Reconciliation
hook_text: Your book says R68 990. The bank says R67 540. Nobody is lying.
clip_script: Think of a savings club. You keep a notebook at home; the treasurer keeps a book at the bank. Month end arrives, you compare, and the numbers differ. Nobody stole a cent. Nobody is lying. The books differ because two people wrote things down at two different moments. Same money, two clocks. That is a building supplies shop and its bank, exactly. But there is a second reason, and it has nothing to do with time: the bank does things to your money without phoning you first. It helps itself to its fees. It drops in a little interest. It runs the standing instructions you signed months ago. And when a customer's transfer bounces because their account was empty, the bank quietly takes that money back out. So sort every line on that statement into three piles. News the bank did that you never wrote down — write it into your journals. Your own slips, like a payment of R5 720 written as R5 270 — fix your book. And things you leave completely alone: the deposit that has not cleared, the transfers that have not gone out. Then ask one question for the bridge: what is the bank still going to do to this? Add what it will add, subtract what it will subtract. Both books land on R68 990.
visual_style: A split screen: a home notebook and a bank statement, items flying into three labelled piles, then a bridge drawing itself between two numbers until both read R68 990; coastal Eastern Cape hardware-yard palette with hand-written ledger textures.
pacing: Fast three-pile sort, then a slow bridge build to the matching totals.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and sort every statement line yourself — three piles, one bridge.
